books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, D. Gender and Family Roles in the Age of the Market Revolution

stimulus.text: Harriet Martineau, an English visitor, wrote in Society in America (1837): “If a test of civilisation be sought, none can be so sure as the condition of that half of society over which the other half has power.” She added: “The Americans have, in the treatment of women, fallen below, not only their own democratic principles, but the practice of some parts of the Old World.” Martineau also wrote that “the sum and substance of female education in America, as in England, is training women to consider marriage as the sole object in life.”
stimulus.source_note: Harriet Martineau, Society in America (1837), chapter “Woman.” Verbatim quotations verified against the Quotidiana transcription of the 1837 text.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Martineau's “test of civilisation” judges a society by

options.text: how those with power treat those without it, especially women
the size of its cities and the volume of its trade
options.misconception: Martineau's test is about power over half of society, not about cities or trade.

options.text: the number of voters who take part in elections
options.misconception: Voting is about men in this period; Martineau's test looks at women, who could not vote.

options.text: the strength of its army and navy
options.misconception: Armies and navies are not Martineau's measure; the condition of women is.

rationales.A: Martineau says the sure test of a civilisation is the condition of the half of society over which the other half has power. Her test looks at women, the half without power.
rationales.B: Cities and trade show prosperity, not justice. Martineau measures a society by how power treats the powerless.
rationales.C: Elections in the 1830s were for white men. A test that only counts voters would miss the women Martineau writes about.
rationales.D: Military strength is not her measure. She tests civilisation by the daily condition of women.
rationales.general:
1. Read her test as a sentence. The condition of the half without power is the measure.
2. Ask who that half is. In her essay it is women, over whom men hold power.
3. Apply the test. Judge America by how women live, not by how rich it is.
Background: Martineau visited the United States in 1834-1836 and published Society in America in 1837, after two years of travel and observation.
Remember: a writer's test tells you what she values, so use her measure, not your own.
